name: Computer Science Foundations
description: The foundational concepts of computational thinking: formal logic, set theory, and recursion — the bedrock upon which all CS is built.

observation.question: What computational patterns do you notice in the world around you?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can identify computational thinking in everyday situations

principle.question: What are the core abstractions that unify all of computer science?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain how logic, sets, and recursion form the foundation

application.question: How do these foundations apply to real software systems?
application.completionEvidence: Student can identify foundational concepts in software artifacts

integration.question: How do these foundations connect to each other and to other disciplines?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can map relationships between foundational concepts

creation.question: How can you combine these foundations to solve novel problems?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can integrate multiple foundational concepts in a solution

content.explanation: Computer science foundations encompass the core abstractions that make computation possible. Logic provides the language of valid reasoning. Set theory provides the mathematics of collections and relationships. Recursion provides the mechanism of self-referential decomposition. Together, they form the bedrock upon which algorithms, data structures, programming languages, and systems are built.
examples: Logic gates implement propositional logic in hardware
Databases store and query sets of records
Compilers use recursion to parse nested syntax
analogies: Foundations are to CS what grammar is to language — invisible when working, obvious when broken
visuals: Map showing how logic → sets → recursion interconnect

practiceProblems.problemText: Identify at least one example of logic, sets, and recursion in a web browser.

memorized.evidence: Can name the three foundational areas
canDo: Identify logic, sets, recursion as foundations

comprehended.evidence: Can explain how each foundation contributes to CS
canDo: Describe the role of each foundation

applied.evidence: Can identify foundational concepts in real software
canDo: Locate logic, sets, recursion in code
cannotDo: Analyze foundational choices in system design

analyzed.evidence: Can decompose systems into foundational components

evaluated.evidence: Can assess when foundational approaches are appropriate

transformed.evidence: Foundational thinking is instinctive — the student sees logic, sets, and recursion everywhere

name: Formal Logic
description: The foundation of computational thinking: propositional and predicate logic, truth tables, logical operators, and proof techniques.

observation.question: What patterns of valid reasoning can you identify in everyday arguments?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can identify premises and conclusions in natural language statements

principle.question: What are the formal rules that make an argument logically valid regardless of its content?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain truth tables, logical operators (AND, OR, NOT, IMPLIES), and validity vs. soundness

application.question: How do you use logical operators to express complex conditions precisely?
application.completionEvidence: Student can translate natural language into propositional logic and evaluate truth values

integration.question: Where does formal logic connect to other domains of reasoning?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can map logical structure to circuit design, database queries, and program control flow

creation.question: How can you construct a novel logical argument that withstands scrutiny?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can construct valid proofs using direct, contrapositive, and contradiction methods

isomorphisms.pattern: conditional branching based on truth values
isomorphisms.mappingDescription: IF-THEN logic maps to base-case checking in recursion
isomorphisms.limitations: Recursion adds temporal depth (calls stack) that static logic does not

content.explanation: Formal logic provides a rigorous framework for reasoning. Propositional logic deals with statements that are true or false, combined using operators like AND (∧), OR (∨), NOT (¬), and IMPLIES (→). A truth table exhaustively maps all possible truth values of compound expressions.
examples: IF it rains THEN the ground is wet (P → Q)
The ground is NOT wet AND it is NOT raining (¬Q ∧ ¬P)
It is raining OR it is cold (P ∨ Q)
nonExamples: It might rain tomorrow (not a logical statement — probabilistic)
Rain feels cold (subjective experience, not truth-functional)
analogies: Logic gates in circuits mirror logical operators
SQL WHERE clauses are applied propositional logic
visuals: Truth table for P → Q showing the only false case: true antecedent, false consequent

practiceProblems.problemText: Construct a truth table for (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P). What is this equivalence called?
Translate into propositional logic: 'If I study and understand the material, then I will pass the exam.'

misconceptions.statement: IF P THEN Q means P causes Q
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: In everyday language, 'if-then' often implies causation
misconceptions.structuralReason: Material conditional only constrains truth values, not causal relationships. P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.

memorized.evidence: Can recall definitions of AND, OR, NOT, IMPLIES from memory
cannotDo: Construct a truth table from scratch

comprehended.evidence: Can explain WHY each operator works the way it does
cannotDo: Identify logical fallacies in complex arguments

applied.evidence: Can translate between natural language and formal logic
cannotDo: Analyze the structure of arguments for hidden assumptions

analyzed.evidence: Can decompose complex arguments into logical components and identify fallacies

evaluated.evidence: Can critically assess the limits of formal logic and choose appropriate frameworks
canDo: Evaluate when logic alone is insufficient

transformed.evidence: Logic has become a lens through which the student sees ALL reasoning — they automatically formalize claims, detect structural weakness, and build airtight arguments in any domain
canDo: Apply logical rigor to any field

name: Set Theory
description: The mathematical foundation of data structures: sets, relations, functions, cardinality, and the algebra of collections.

observation.question: How do you naturally group and categorize things in your daily life?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can identify examples of sets, subsets, and membership in everyday contexts

principle.question: What are the formal operations that govern how collections interact?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can define union, intersection, difference, complement, and power set

application.question: How do you use set operations to solve real computational problems?
application.completionEvidence: Student can solve problems involving Venn diagrams, counting, and set-builder notation

integration.question: How do sets connect to logic, databases, and type systems?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can map set operations to SQL JOINs, logical connectives, and type intersections

creation.question: How can you model a complex real-world system using set-theoretic structures?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can formalize a domain model using sets, relations, and functions

isomorphisms.mappingDescription: Set operations (union, intersection) parallel logical connectives (OR, AND)
isomorphisms.limitations: Sets deal with membership; logic deals with truth values

content.explanation: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct elements. Set theory provides the language for describing collections and their relationships. Core operations include union (A ∪ B), intersection (A ∩ B), difference (A \ B), and complement (A'). Functions are special relations where each input maps to exactly one output.
examples: A function f: ℕ → ℕ where f(n) = n²
nonExamples: A list with duplicate elements (multiset, not a set)
A vague collection like 'tall people' (not well-defined)
analogies: SQL tables are finite sets of rows
TypeScript union types (A | B) model set union
Database INNER JOIN is set intersection
visuals: Venn diagram showing A ∩ B and A ∪ B
Mapping diagram of a function vs. a relation

practiceProblems.problemText: Given A = {1,2,3,4} and B = {3,4,5,6}, find A ∩ B, A ∪ B, and A \ B.
Explain why the power set of {1,2,3} has exactly 8 elements.

misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Lists and arrays allow duplicates, and we often think of collections that way
misconceptions.structuralReason: By definition, a set contains each element exactly once. Duplicates collapse. This is what distinguishes sets from multisets or lists.

memorized.evidence: Can recall definitions of set, union, intersection, difference

comprehended.evidence: Can explain how set operations work and why they matter

applied.evidence: Can use set operations to solve concrete problems
canDo: Translate word problems to set notation
cannotDo: Analyze the structure of set systems

analyzed.evidence: Can decompose complex systems into set-theoretic components
canDo: Map set operations to logical connectives

evaluated.evidence: Can assess the appropriateness of set-theoretic models for different problems

transformed.evidence: Set theory has become an intuitive lens — the student naturally thinks in terms of collections, relations, and mappings across all domains

name: Recursion
description: The self-referential heart of computation: recursive definitions, divide-and-conquer, and the relationship between recursion and induction.

observation.question: Where do you see self-similar patterns repeating in nature or daily life?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can identify examples of recursive structure (fractals, nested containers, family trees)

principle.question: What are the minimal components that make a recursive definition well-founded?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain base case, recursive case, and the necessity of termination

application.question: How do you decompose a problem into smaller instances of itself?
application.completionEvidence: Student can write recursive functions and trace their execution through the call stack

integration.question: How does recursion connect to mathematical induction, trees, and self-reference?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can prove correctness via induction and map recursion to tree traversal

creation.question: How can you design a novel recursive solution that elegantly decomposes a complex problem?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can design and implement a divide-and-conquer algorithm for a novel problem

isomorphisms.mappingDescription: Recursive base cases parallel logical base truths; recursive cases parallel logical deduction chains
isomorphisms.limitations: Recursion adds execution order and stack depth; logic is timeless

isomorphisms.pattern: combining smaller instances into a whole
isomorphisms.mappingDescription: Divide-and-conquer splits a set into subsets; union recombines results
isomorphisms.limitations: Sets are flat; recursion creates hierarchical structure

content.explanation: Recursion is a method where the solution depends on solutions to smaller instances of the same problem. A well-formed recursive function has a base case (termination condition) and a recursive case (calls itself with a smaller input). The call stack manages the chain of pending computations.
examples: Tree traversal: visit left, visit root, visit right
nonExamples: An infinite loop without a base case (not recursion, just repetition)
Iterative loops (recursion uses self-reference, iteration uses state mutation)
analogies: A dictionary that defines words using other words — eventually you reach words you already know (base case)
visuals: Call stack diagram showing nested calls unwinding

practiceProblems.problemText: Write a recursive function to compute the sum of a list. Identify the base case and recursive case.
Trace the execution of fib(5) showing all recursive calls. How many calls are made?

misconceptions.statement: Recursion is always slower than iteration
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Function calls have overhead; loops don't
misconceptions.structuralReason: While individual calls have overhead, recursive algorithms can have better time complexity (e.g., merge sort O(n log n) vs. naive O(n²)). Tail-call optimization eliminates overhead in many languages.

misconceptions.statement: You need to understand the entire call stack to write recursion
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Tracing recursive calls is mentally demanding
misconceptions.structuralReason: The trust-the-protocol principle: if the recursive call works correctly for smaller inputs, and the base case is correct, the whole function is correct. You don't need to trace the full stack.

memorized.evidence: Can recall the definition of recursion and identify base/recursive cases in given code
canDo: Name the components of a recursive function

comprehended.evidence: Can explain HOW recursion works (call stack, unwinding) and WHY it terminates
cannotDo: Design recursive solutions to novel problems

applied.evidence: Can write correct recursive functions for standard problems

analyzed.evidence: Can decompose complex problems into recursive sub-problems and analyze their properties

evaluated.evidence: Can assess when recursion is the right tool and evaluate the quality of recursive designs
canDo: Judge the elegance of recursive solutions

transformed.evidence: Recursive thinking has become natural — the student sees self-similar structure everywhere and instinctively decomposes problems hierarchically
canDo: See recursive structure in non-CS domains
